questions.question_text: A horizontal force of $5$ N is applied on a stationary body of mass $5$ kg, which is initially at rest on a frictionless table. The change in kinetic energy of the body in $10$ s is
questions.question_html: A horizontal force of $5$ N is applied on a stationary body of mass $5$ kg, which is initially at rest on a frictionless table. The change in kinetic energy of the body in $10$ s is
questions.explanation_text: The body is on a frictionless table, so the applied force produces acceleration without any loss due to friction. Given, $F=5\text{N}$ $m=5\text{kg}$ Using Newton’s second law, $F=ma$ So, $a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{5}{5}=1\text{m s}^{-2}$ The body starts from rest, so $u=0$ Time, $t=10\text{s}$ Using $v=u+at$ we get $v=0+1 \times 10=10\text{m s}^{-1}$ Initial kinetic energy is zero because the body is initially at rest. Final kinetic energy is $K=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ $K=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times (10)^{2}$ $K=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 100=250\text{J}$ So, the change in kinetic energy of the body in $10$ s is $250\text{J}$ Correct option: Option D.
questions.explanation_html:
The body is on a frictionless table, so the applied force produces acceleration without any loss due to friction.

Given,

$F=5\text{N}$

$m=5\text{kg}$

Using Newton’s second law,

$F=ma$

So,

$a=\frac{F}{m}=\frac{5}{5}=1\text{m s}^{-2}$

The body starts from rest, so

$u=0$

Time,

$t=10\text{s}$

Using

$v=u+at$

we get

$v=0+1 \times 10=10\text{m s}^{-1}$

Initial kinetic energy is zero because the body is initially at rest.

Final kinetic energy is

$K=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

$K=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times (10)^{2}$

$K=\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 100=250\text{J}$

So, the change in kinetic energy of the body in $10$ s is

$250\text{J}$

Correct option: Option D.

questions.question_text: Two bodies with kinetic energies in the ratio of $3:1$ are moving with equal linear momentum. The ratio of their masses is
questions.question_html: Two bodies with kinetic energies in the ratio of $3:1$ are moving with equal linear momentum. The ratio of their masses is
questions.explanation_text: For a body having momentum $p$ and mass $m$ , kinetic energy is $K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ Here, both bodies have equal linear momentum, so $p$ is the same for both. So kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass: $K∝\frac{1}{m}$ Given, $K_{1}:K_{2}=3:1$ So, $\frac{K_{1}}{K_{2}}=\frac{m_{2}}{m_{1}}$ $\frac{3}{1}=\frac{m_{2}}{m_{1}}$ Hence, $m_{1}:m_{2}=1:3$ The ratio of their masses is $1:3$ So the correct option is Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
For a body having momentum $p$ and mass $m$ , kinetic energy is

$K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$

Here, both bodies have equal linear momentum, so $p$ is the same for both.

So kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass:

$K∝\frac{1}{m}$

Given,

$K_{1}:K_{2}=3:1$

So,

$\frac{K_{1}}{K_{2}}=\frac{m_{2}}{m_{1}}$

$\frac{3}{1}=\frac{m_{2}}{m_{1}}$

Hence,

$m_{1}:m_{2}=1:3$

The ratio of their masses is

$1:3$

So the correct option is Option B.

questions.question_text: A body of mass 0.25 kg travels along a straight line from $x=0$ to $x=2m$ with a speed $v=kx^{3/2}$ where $k$ $=2SI$ units. The work done by the net during this displacement is
questions.question_html: A body of mass 0.25 kg travels along a straight line from $x=0$ to $x=2m$ with a speed $v=kx^{3/2}$ where $k$ $=2SI$ units. The work done by the net during this displacement is
questions.explanation_text: To determine the work done by the net force during the displacement of the body, we need to evaluate the change in kinetic energy (ΔKE) as the object moves from $x=0$ to $x=2\text{m}$ . The initial velocity $u$ when $x=0$ is zero because $v=kx^{3/2}$ and substituting $x=0$ gives $v=0$ . The final kinetic energy at $x=2\text{m}$ can be found by calculating the velocity at this point: $v=k \cdot (2)^{3/2}$ Given $k=2\text{SI units}$ , the velocity at $x=2$ is: $v=2 \cdot 2^{3/2}$ The change in kinetic energy is: $\Delta\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}-\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}$ Substituting $m=0.25\text{kg}$ and $u=0$ : $\Delta\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times (2 \times 2^{3/2})^{2}-0$ Calculate $(2 \times 2^{3/2})^{2}$ : $=(2^{1} \times (2^{3/2}))^{2}=2^{2} \times (2^{3})=2^{5}=32$ So the change in kinetic energy is: $\Delta\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times 32$ Finally, solving gives: $=4\text{J}$ Hence, the work done by the net force during the displacement is 4 Joules.
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the work done by the net force during the displacement of the body, we need to evaluate the change in kinetic energy (ΔKE) as the object moves from $x=0$ to $x=2\text{m}$ .

The initial velocity $u$ when $x=0$ is zero because $v=kx^{3/2}$ and substituting $x=0$ gives $v=0$ .

The final kinetic energy at $x=2\text{m}$ can be found by calculating the velocity at this point:

$v=k \cdot (2)^{3/2}$

Given $k=2\text{SI units}$ , the velocity at $x=2$ is:

$v=2 \cdot 2^{3/2}$

The change in kinetic energy is:

$\Delta\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}-\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}$

Substituting $m=0.25\text{kg}$ and $u=0$ :

$\Delta\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times (2 \times 2^{3/2})^{2}-0$

Calculate $(2 \times 2^{3/2})^{2}$ :

$=(2^{1} \times (2^{3/2}))^{2}=2^{2} \times (2^{3})=2^{5}=32$

So the change in kinetic energy is:

$\Delta\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times 32$

Finally, solving gives:

$=4\text{J}$

Hence, the work done by the net force during the displacement is 4 Joules.

questions.question_text: A ball of mass $0.2kg$ is thrown vertically down from a height of $10m$ . It collides with the floor and loses $50%$ of its energy and then rises back to the same height. The value of its initial velocity is
questions.question_html: A ball of mass $0.2kg$ is thrown vertically down from a height of $10m$ . It collides with the floor and loses $50%$ of its energy and then rises back to the same height. The value of its initial velocity is
questions.explanation_text: Given, mass of the ball, $m=0.2kg$ Height from the surface of floor, $ℎ=10m$ Let initial velocity be $u$ . Total energy as initial point $TE=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+mgℎ$ After collision, remaining energy $=\frac{\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}+mgℎ}{2}$ With this remaining energy the ball bounces upto height $ℎ$ Therefore, $\frac{\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}+mgℎ}{2}=mgℎ$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}mu^{2}+mgℎ=2mgℎ \\ & \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow u^{2} & =\sqrt{2gℎ} \\ & =\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 10}=14m/s \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, mass of the ball, $m=0.2kg$

Height from the surface of floor, $ℎ=10m$

Let initial velocity be $u$ .

Total energy as initial point $TE=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}+mgℎ$

After collision, remaining energy

$=\frac{\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}+mgℎ}{2}$

With this remaining energy the ball bounces upto height $ℎ$

Therefore, $\frac{\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}+mgℎ}{2}=mgℎ$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}mu^{2}+mgℎ=2mgℎ \\ & \begin{aligned} \Rightarrow u^{2} & =\sqrt{2gℎ} \\ & =\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 10}=14m/s \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: A smooth chain of length $2m$ is kept on a table such that its length of $60cm$ hangs freely from the edge of the table. The total mass of the chain is $4kg$ . The work done in pulling the entire chain on the table is (Take, $g=10m/s^{2}$ )
questions.explanation_text: Mass per unit length of chain, $\frac{M}{L}=\frac{4}{2}=2kg/m$ Work done in pulling the chain of small length $dx$ , $\begin{aligned} dW & =\text{mass of length}dx \times g \times x \\ & =\frac{M}{L} \times dx \times g \times x \\ & =2 \times dx \times 10 \times x=20xdx \end{aligned}$ Work done, $W=\int_{0}^{0.6}dWdx=\int_{0}^{0.6}20xdx$ $=[20\frac{x^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{0.6}=[10x^{2}]_{0}^{0.6}=10 \times (0.6)^{2}=3.6J$

$\frac{M}{L}=\frac{4}{2}=2kg/m$

Work done in pulling the chain of small length $dx$ ,

$\begin{aligned} dW & =\text{mass of length}dx \times g \times x \\ & =\frac{M}{L} \times dx \times g \times x \\ & =2 \times dx \times 10 \times x=20xdx \end{aligned}$

Work done, $W=\int_{0}^{0.6}dWdx=\int_{0}^{0.6}20xdx$

$=[20\frac{x^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{0.6}=[10x^{2}]_{0}^{0.6}=10 \times (0.6)^{2}=3.6J$

questions.question_text: Two particles of masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of their momentum is
questions.question_html: Two particles of masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of their momentum is
questions.explanation_text: Let's break down the problem step by step: The kinetic energy for a particle is given by: $K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$ Since both particles have equal kinetic energies: $\frac{p_{1}^{2}}{2m_{1}}=\frac{p_{2}^{2}}{2m_{2}}$ Eliminating the common factor of 2, we have: $\frac{p_{1}^{2}}{m_{1}}=\frac{p_{2}^{2}}{m_{2}}$ Rearranging the equation to solve for the ratio of the momenta: $\frac{p_{1}^{2}}{p_{2}^{2}}=\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}$ Taking the square root of both sides gives: $\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}}$ This means the ratio of the momentum of particle 1 to that of particle 2 is: $p_{1}:p_{2}=\sqrt{m_{1}}:\sqrt{m_{2}}$ Thus, the correct option is: Option C $\sqrt{m_{1}}:\sqrt{m_{2}}$
questions.explanation_html:
Let's break down the problem step by step:

The kinetic energy for a particle is given by:

$K=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}$

Since both particles have equal kinetic energies:

$\frac{p_{1}^{2}}{2m_{1}}=\frac{p_{2}^{2}}{2m_{2}}$

Eliminating the common factor of 2, we have:

$\frac{p_{1}^{2}}{m_{1}}=\frac{p_{2}^{2}}{m_{2}}$

Rearranging the equation to solve for the ratio of the momenta:

$\frac{p_{1}^{2}}{p_{2}^{2}}=\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}$

Taking the square root of both sides gives:

$\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_{1}}{m_{2}}}$

This means the ratio of the momentum of particle 1 to that of particle 2 is:

$p_{1}:p_{2}=\sqrt{m_{1}}:\sqrt{m_{2}}$

Thus, the correct option is:

Option C

$\sqrt{m_{1}}:\sqrt{m_{2}}$

questions.question_text: A motor pump lifts 6 tonnes of water from a well of depth 25 m to the first floor of height 35 m from the ground floor in 20 minutes. The power of the pump (in kW ) is $[g=10ms^{-2}$ ]
questions.question_html: A motor pump lifts 6 tonnes of water from a well of depth 25 m to the first floor of height 35 m from the ground floor in 20 minutes. The power of the pump (in kW ) is $[g=10ms^{-2}$ ]
questions.explanation_text: Given: Water lifted: 6 tonnes (6000 kg) Depth of well: 25 m Height of first floor: 35 m Time taken: 20 minutes (or 1200 seconds) Gravitational acceleration: $g=10\text{m/s}^{2}$ To find the power of the pump: Calculate the work done: The work done in lifting the water is given by the formula: $\text{Work}=m \times g \times ℎ$ Here, $ℎ$ is the height difference from the well to the first floor, which is $35\text{m}-25\text{m}=10\text{m}$ . Substitute the values: $\text{Work}=6000 \times 10 \times 10=600,000\text{Joules}$ Calculate the power: Power is the rate at which work is done and is given by the formula: $P=\frac{\text{Work}}{\text{Time}}$ Substituting the work and time: $P=\frac{600,000}{1200}=500\text{W}$ $P=3,000\text{W}=3\text{kW}$ Therefore, the power of the pump is $3\text{kW}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
Given:

Water lifted: 6 tonnes (6000 kg)

Depth of well: 25 m

Height of first floor: 35 m

Time taken: 20 minutes (or 1200 seconds)

Gravitational acceleration: $g=10\text{m/s}^{2}$

To find the power of the pump:

Calculate the work done:

The work done in lifting the water is given by the formula:

$\text{Work}=m \times g \times ℎ$

Here, $ℎ$ is the height difference from the well to the first floor, which is $35\text{m}-25\text{m}=10\text{m}$ .

Substitute the values:

$\text{Work}=6000 \times 10 \times 10=600,000\text{Joules}$

Calculate the power:

Power is the rate at which work is done and is given by the formula:

$P=\frac{\text{Work}}{\text{Time}}$

Substituting the work and time:

$P=\frac{600,000}{1200}=500\text{W}$

$P=3,000\text{W}=3\text{kW}$

Therefore, the power of the pump is $3\text{kW}$ .
